title: Envision Glasses read street signs, menus and scenes for Wes Ramage in Calgary, bringing comfort he had not had in years
summary: Globe and Mail, 26 Dec 2023: Wes Ramage of Calgary uses Envision Glasses (Google Glass plus Envision's AI) to read signs for transit, read menus, find chairs and objects and describe scenes.
account: In a Globe and Mail report of 26 December 2023, Joe Castaldo described how Wes Ramage of Calgary, who is blind, uses Envision Glasses, a Google Glass headset running Envision's AI software, to describe scenes, identify clothing colors, find empty chairs and misplaced objects, read street signs when navigating transit and read menus; Ramage said the glasses bring a level of comfort he had not had in many years and described heading out each morning with his glasses, keys and wallet. The article gives a price of US$1,899 to US$3,499, accessed in his case through a provincial assistance program, and also profiles Nayla Farah of Toronto using the Be My AI app, which is covered by an existing record. Envision's product page states that the glasses are built on Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2 and offer Instant Text, Scan Text, Describe Scene and an Ask Envision feature on an OpenAI model. The date observed is the article's publication date; the article does not date the individual uses.
purpose: Envision Glasses are built to speak out text and surroundings for blind and low-vision users; reading signs and menus is that purpose.
system: Envision Glasses: Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2 running Envision's text recognition, scene description and Ask Envision features
segment: Blind and low-vision users (wearable reading assistant)
taxonomy_note: Personal depth 1 as for AIBD-0034 (Be My AI): daily-living tasks reported by a named user in an independent news report, with no measured outcome. The Globe article names ChatGPT and GPT-4 among underlying models in general; Envision's page, as fetched in October 2026, says Ask Envision uses GPT-5, so the model in use in 2023 is not fixed by the sources and the model version is null.

ratings.reason: A named user reads signs, menus and scenes independently and reports lasting comfort; a small daily-living benefit documented by a reporter, not measured.

ai_role.statement: The glasses' text recognition and scene description produced the readings Ramage relies on; the Globe article is the only outcome source and attributes the comfort to the glasses in the user's own words. No clinical or task measurement exists in the fetched sources.

evidence.title: For some blind and low-vision people, AI glasses unlock a new independence

headline: Envision Glasses read street signs and menus for Wes Ramage

comparator.before: Before, a bus would drive right by me because I'm standing at a yield sign
comparator.after: Now he can ask the glasses for a description to ensure he's in the right place.
comparator.quote: "Before, a bus would drive right by me because I'm standing at a yield sign," he said. Now he can ask the glasses for a description to ensure he's in the right place. "That brings a level of comfort I have not had in so many years."

later.note: Envision's product page, read on 21 October 2026, still sells the glasses and now says Ask Envision uses GPT-5 by OpenAI, so the product continued with a newer model; the page does not date the change.
later.quote: Introducing "Ask Envision", a revolutionary feature that enables people who are blind or low-vision to scan documents and ask questions using GPT-5 by OpenAI.
